Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Chad predominantly use paper registers for patient data recording at the point of service. Aggregate data from these paper records is collated monthly and forwarded to district levels, where it is entered digitally into DHIS2, with 96% of districts now reporting directly into the system as of 2022.DHIS2 Chad transition. A 2021 study in Massaguet district (including rural health centres) confirmed routine use of paper-based external consultation registers and HMIS forms, with data digitized only at district level using Excel; no EMR at clinics, and paper stock-outs common, leading to inaccuracies.BMC study Massaguet. No evidence found of routine digital entry, EMR, or DHIS2 at point of care in rural clinics; plans exist for tablets in northern regions for offline DHIS2 aggregate entry, but not implemented widely.DHIS2 Chad transition. Key barriers: poor internet/power in rural north, staff workload, form stock-outs, low digital literacy. National ambition via DHIS2 rollout contrasts with rural paper reality; pilots/digital limited to aggregation, not point-of-service.

revision_notes: Original sources (DHIS2 transition note, 2021 Massaguet BMC study) were fetched and confirm paper-based registers with digitisation occurring only at district level, not at the clinic. A further search identified documented facility-level digital data capture: a tablet-based clinical decision support system (CDSS), piloted as SysRef from 2019 in three rural primary healthcare facilities in southern Chad and now operating as SANU-TD (Sante Numerique au Tchad), with health workers entering patient consultation data directly onto tablets at point of care (offline, synced later). A May 2024 Geneva Health Forum poster confirms the tool is being extended to the national health system in southern Chad under the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation-funded PADS programme. This is genuine facility-level digital capture, not just aggregation, though still confined to a subset of rural clinics in the south alongside the still-dominant paper-register system documented in Massaguet district and the DHIS2 rollout. Recalculated from 1 (Entirely paper) to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). Year set to 2024 based on the most recent evidence (medium confidence, as the national scale of the pilot is not quantified).
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Chad remain predominantly paper-based, with patient consultations recorded in paper registers and HMIS forms that are aggregated and entered electronically only at district level (DHIS2, with 96% of districts reporting directly as of 2022). Facility-level digital data capture nonetheless exists in a small but growing subset of rural clinics: a tablet-based clinical decision support system, piloted as SysRef (2019-2023) in three primary healthcare facilities in southern Chad and now operating as SANU-TD, enables health workers to record consultations digitally at the point of care, and the tool is being extended to the national health system in southern health districts under the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation-funded PADS programme. Barriers to wider digitisation include poor rural connectivity and power supply and low digital literacy, meaning paper remains the norm outside these pilot districts.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Evidence suggests rural police stations in Chad are still predominantly paper-based, with digitisation happening mainly at central level. INTERPOL's EU-funded Chad Police Information System (SIPT) (a WAPIS-like system) was created to move away from paper records and provide a centralized computerized database for police data (persons, offences, vehicles, documents), managed via a Data Collection/Registration Center (DACORE/CREDOP) that records and validates police data; INTERPOL notes longer-term plans to deploy access to the system across agencies and regions/border posts depending on infrastructure, implying that broad station-level digital entry is not yet universal. Recent US State Department human rights reporting describes police and detention procedures but does not indicate routine digital case/complaint recording, consistent with continued reliance on traditional paper proces-verbaux at station level, especially outside N'Djamena. Overall: predominantly paper at rural stations, with some digitalisation through SIPT at national/central nodes and potential roll-out pilots.

revision_notes: Confirmed score of 1 (Entirely paper). The original WAPIS brochure was fetched and confirms the programme's stated purpose of moving Chad away from paper police records via a single centralised DACORE. Fresher sources (WAPIS Newsletter, late 2024; Alwihda Info, July 2025) show the Chad Police Information System (SIPT) remains in a 'final phase' of implementation as of mid-2025: the DACORE and Forensic Science building renovation and the AFIS fingerprint technology roll-out were still under way in 2024-2025, the legal/data-protection framework was only finalised in January 2024, and the project has been extended to December 2025 following earlier delays from political instability. Digitisation remains centred on the single national DACORE facility, with no evidence of digital case recording at station level, particularly in rural areas. Year updated to 2025 (high confidence) reflecting the most recent status reporting available.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Chad remain paper-based for day-to-day case and complaint recording. The EU-funded, INTERPOL-implemented Chad Police Information System (SIPT), a WAPIS-type programme, centres on a single Data Collection and Registration Centre (DACORE), which was still completing infrastructure renovation and rolling out an Automated Fingerprint Identification System as of mid-2025, with the project extended to December 2025. Legal and governance frameworks for the SIPT were only finalised in January 2024, and implementation has historically been delayed by political instability. There is no evidence that digital case recording extends to police stations outside the central DACORE, and traditional paper proces-verbaux continue to be used at station level, particularly outside N'Djamena.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Chad record administrative data, attendance (annual snapshots), and proxies for learning outcomes (repetition/pass rates) using handwritten paper questionnaires and registers. School directors and teachers manually fill 4-10 page EMIS forms covering enrollment by class/gender/age/status, infrastructure, teachers, materials, finances. These paper forms are physically transported upward through a hierarchical structure: school -> zone inspectors -> district -> provincial -> national DAPRO, where data is entered digitally via StatEduc2 software.UNESCO ECW Chad EMIS Case Study No evidence of digital tools at point-of-service; process remains fully manual at rural facilities, with last full survey in 2016 and 2019 requiring special national efforts due to logistics. Digital systems like national EMIS database exist for aggregation, but rural recording is paper-based transcription later. Limited pilots: UNICEF EduTrac SMS/mobile in 2 provinces (not scaled); no widespread adoption.UNESCO ECW Chad EMIS Case Study;World Bank Chad Learning Poverty Brief Key barriers: vast rural distances/poor transport, lack of subnational capacity/training/verification, no feedback to schools causing fatigue, French-only forms in Arabic areas, no birth certificates for accurate age/enrollment. Gap: National EMIS strategy (2014)/sector plans aspire to better data, but rural reality lags due to infrastructure/human resources; digital ambitions (e.g., ecole.cnc.td platform) focus on content, not POS recording.UNESCO IICBA Chad Brief

revision_notes: Confirmed score of 1 (Entirely paper). The original UNESCO EMIS case study and World Bank Learning Poverty brief were fetched and support the description of paper-based data collection with central digitisation only. A 2025 UNICEF Innocenti account of Chad's EMIS confirms the system remains structured around paper-based data collection at the 12,863 primary schools nationwide (2025 figure), transmitted up a hierarchical chain (school - zone inspectorate - district - province - national DAPRO) with digital entry, via StatEduc2 software, occurring only at the DAPRO level; decentralisation efforts (already effective in 16 of 23 provinces, extending to 7 more under the PRET programme) concern data compilation and use, not point-of-service digital capture. A 2023 Global Partnership for Education independent technical assessment (ITAP) likewise confirms paper-based Statistical Yearbook data collection nationally. No evidence found of digital data capture devices in routine use at rural primary schools; the previously noted UNICEF EduTrac pilot has not been scaled. Year updated to 2025 (high confidence).
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Chad record enrolment, attendance, and administrative data on paper questionnaires and registers completed manually by school directors and teachers. These paper forms pass through a hierarchical administrative chain (school, zone inspectorate, district, province, national Direction des Affaires de la Planification, de la Recherche et de l'Organisation scolaires - DAPRO), with digital entry, via the StatEduc2 software, occurring only at the DAPRO level. As of 2025, Chad has 12,863 primary schools nationally, and while the Ministry of National Education and Civic Promotion has begun decentralising education management information system (EMIS) functions to 16 of 23 provinces (extending to a further seven under the Programme for the Refoundation of Chadian Schools), this concerns data compilation and use rather than point-of-service digital recording. No evidence indicates digital data capture tools are used at rural school level; limited pilots such as UNICEF's EduTrac in two provinces have not been scaled nationally.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Chad predominantly use paper-based systems for birth registration. Recent data shows only 26% national birth registration rate among under-5s, with 84% of children rural and significantly lower rates in rural vs urban areas (largest gaps in Chad per UAPS 2024 analysis), indicating poor coverage and likely manual recording at remote points. A UNICEF-supported Tasdjil digital app (launched 2022, offline-capable, <10 min process) has enabled 109k+ registrations, often at health facilities, representing a donor pilot to boost access. No evidence of majority rural facilities using digital point-of-service; paper remains default. Barriers: remoteness (Chad 80%+ rural), poverty, low awareness, infrastructure deficits. National efforts (e.g., centers, campaigns) exist but gap persists between policy and rural reality-digital limited to pilots, not scaled/standardized at rural registries. Score conservative due to thin specific evidence on recording methods.

revision_notes: Confirmed score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). The original UAPS abstract and UNICEF USA story were fetched and support the description of low overall birth registration with a UNICEF-backed digital pilot (Tasdjil). A Global Financing Facility knowledge platform page confirms civil registration in Chad 'is evolving very slowly,' with the 2019 MICS6 survey recording a 25.5% national birth registration rate (50% urban versus 21.1% rural) and near non-existent death/marriage registration; digitisation of civil status records 'is being piloted in a few health districts' with UNICEF, UNFPA and UNHCR, not yet standard practice. The Tasdjil digital app (offline-capable, sub-10-minute registration, launched 2022) had driven over 109,000 registrations by mid-2024, and one-stop birth registration offices integrating Tasdjil into health facilities (e.g. Bol, Lake Province, opened November 2023) continue to expand, with further reform activity reported into 2025 (Biometric Update, June 2025). This supports a 'some digital' characterisation alongside a still-dominant paper/manual process at most rural registry points. Year updated to 2025 (medium confidence, since the underlying quantitative coverage figure dates to 2019 MICS6 while programme status evidence is current to 2025).
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Chad rely predominantly on paper-based processes, reflected in a national birth registration rate of just 25.5% among under-fives (2019 MICS6), with a pronounced urban-rural gap (50% urban versus 21.1% rural) and death and marriage registration described as almost non-existent. Digitisation of civil status records is being piloted in a limited number of health districts in partnership with UNICEF, UNFPA and UNHCR, most visibly through the offline-capable Tasdjil mobile application (launched 2022), which has enabled over 109,000 birth registrations by linking registration to health facility visits, and through one-stop birth registration offices such as that opened in Bol, Lake Province, in November 2023. These initiatives represent meaningful but geographically limited pockets of digital capture; most rural registry points continue to depend on manual paper-based recording, and coverage remains low overall.
